\section{Retrieval error and the transmission profile}\label{sec:results-transfer}

Theorem~\ref{thm:transfer} makes the reflectance error at an entry a function of two things, the retrieval-weighted
component error $e_R$ and the transmission $t$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:profile} makes the rate a function of where
$e_R$ sits relative to $t$. Table~\ref{tab:v2-transmission} reports, for the wide-network heads of
Section~\ref{sec:scaling} on the test rows of each split, the quantities those theorems name: $\varepsilon_R$ and the
exponent $2\nu$ of the conditional profile $t\mapsto\E[e_R^2\mid t]$ fitted over the observed transmission range,
the raw inverse \eqref{eq:inv} with its non-finite and non-positive-denominator failures, the constrained retrieval
\eqref{eq:rhobar} with its failures and clips, the pointwise quantity $\E\min\{R^2,e_R^2/t^2\}$, the number of
entries at which the pointwise inequality of Theorem~\ref{thm:transfer}(i) fails, and the ratio of the middle bound
of Theorem~\ref{thm:transfer}(ii), minimised over a threshold ladder, to the measured mean-square error of the
constrained retrieval. The albedo bound $S$ is the largest physical value on the training rows; the table carries
454 training entries with spherical albedo above one, all in deep absorption bands at vanishing flux, which are
outside the hypothesis and are counted rather than used, and no held-out entry exceeds $S$. The surface reflectance
is $\rho=0.7$ and $R=0.9$.

\IfFileExists{table_v2_transmission.tex}{
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{\input{table_v2_transmission}}
\caption{Transmission-conditioned retrieval on the wide-network heads at $\rho=0.7$: the retrieval-weighted error,
the observed-range profile exponent, the raw and constrained inverses with their failure and clip rates, the
pointwise bound of Theorem~\ref{thm:transfer}, its violation count over the test entries, and the ratio of the
distributional bound to the measured error. Mean and standard deviation over the splits listed in the file.}
\label{tab:v2-transmission}
\end{table}}{}

The table's columns line up with the theorem. The retrieval-weighted error $\varepsilon_R$ runs from $0.047$ for the
kernel on features to $0.166$ for the single network; the observed-range profile exponents lie between $0.16$ and
$0.28$; the pointwise inequality of Theorem~\ref{thm:transfer}(i) is violated at no test entry of any head; and the
distributional bound of item (ii), minimised over the threshold ladder, exceeds the measured mean-square error of the
constrained retrieval by a factor between $3.6$ and $5.3$, the slack being the tail mass term. The raw inverse and
the constrained retrieval separate the heads in the same order but at different scales: the raw 95th percentile is
$0.06$--$0.10$ for the feature kernels and the selection against $0.46$--$0.70$ for the networks and the input kernel,
and the constrained 95th percentile $0.06$--$0.15$ against $0.20$--$0.27$, with $0.6$ to $1.2\%$ of the entries
failing the positivity test and $1.5$ to $3.6\%$ clipped at $R$. Three facts carry the comparison between the
feature kernel and its stack. One entry in twenty has transmission
below $3\times10^{-4}$ of the training flux scale and one in a hundred below $10^{-10}$; the observed-range tail
slope of $F_t$ is about $0.23$. The absolute component errors of every head are not concentrated at low
transmission: the share of $\varepsilon_R^2$ below $0.03$ of the scale is under a thousandth for every head. The
retrieval tails are therefore produced by dividing an ordinary absolute error by a vanishing $t$, which is the
mechanism of Theorem~\ref{thm:transfer}(i), and the all-band 95th and 99th percentiles measure the opaque bands
rather than the heads. The profile exponents in the table, between $0.17$ and $0.34$ on the observed range, are far
from the value $2\nu=2$ at which Theorem~\ref{thm:profile} gives a rate without loss, so on the all-band
distribution the rate loss of Theorem~\ref{thm:transfer}(iii) is the operative regime, while on a passband
$t\ge t_0$ the error transfers at the rate of the components by Theorem~\ref{thm:transfer}(iv). The comparison
between heads is accordingly made decile by decile in transmission and on the constrained retrieval, whose error is
bounded by $R$ and is covered by Proposition~\ref{prop:selection}; the raw inverse and its failure counts are
reported beside it.

\section{Representation, correction and combination}\label{sec:results-representation}

\IfFileExists{table_v2_replication.tex}{Table~\ref{tab:v2-replication} replicates the three-member concatenated-feature kernel of Section~\ref{sec:scaling}
at four further splits, with the three members trained at width 2{,}000 for 500 epochs and every prediction stored in

single member's features; the paired gain is $0.0076\pm0.0053$ radiance points, positive at three of the four splits
and $-0.0002$ at the fourth. Its median reflectance error is $0.033$ points against $0.040$, and its within-split
95th percentile $6.0$ points against $7.5$: at these splits the concatenation improves the tail as well as the mean.
The convex stack of the two kernels and the residual-corrected network has the same mean radiance error as the
concatenated kernel ($0.069\%$) and a 95th percentile of $14$ points, the tail cost of stacking seen in
Section~\ref{sec:scaling}; the residual-corrected network alone stands at $0.157\%$ and $49$ points. The
split-level pairing is the unit of comparison; the test sets overlap and the standard deviations describe the spread
over splits, not confidence intervals.}{}

\IfFileExists{table_v2_stacks.tex}{
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{\input{table_v2_stacks}}
\caption{Combinations of the heads fitted on the validation rows and read once on the test rows, at $\rho=0.7$:
the single heads, the stack under the mean relative norm per component (the objective of the campaign stack), the
stack under the row-relative squared error, and the stack under $J_\tau$ of \eqref{eq:Jtau} on projected heads at
several thresholds. Mean and standard deviation over the lanes listed in the file.}
\label{tab:v2-stacks}
\end{table}}{}

The stacking objective decides the albedo head. Under any squared objective, whether in physical units or
row-relative, the simplex weight on the spherical albedo goes to the network, whose albedo error is smaller in
mean square, and the radiance error of the combination is worse than the feature kernel alone: the stack under the
row-relative squared error reaches $0.113\%$ against $0.076\%$ for the kernel on features and $0.069\%$ for the kernel
on concatenated features. Under the mean relative norm the weight goes to the kernel, whose albedo errors are mostly
small with a heavier tail, and the combination ties the single-member feature kernel ($0.075\%$) without reaching the
concatenated kernel. The retrieval tails move the other way: the constrained 95th percentile of the mean-relative
stack is $0.14$ against $0.06$ for the concatenated kernel and $0.08$ for the single-member kernel, so the stack that
matches the kernel's forward error does not match its inverse tail. The theorem's objective $J_\tau$ inherits the
squared form and therefore the network's albedo; its promise is the bound \eqref{eq:Jtau-bound}, not a forward
improvement, and the table shows the price: $0.22$--$0.23\%$ radiance error for $\tau\le0.1$, $0.15\%$ at
$\tau=0.3$ and $0.12\%$ at $\tau\ge1$, with constrained 95th percentiles between $0.10$ and $0.17$ and the 99th
percentile at the clip $R=0.7$ except at $\tau$ between $0.01$ and $0.1$, where it falls to $0.59\pm0.22$. The
threshold $\tau$ is fixed before the test read, with the validation coverage $F_t(\tau)$ it implies recorded in the
file.

\IfFileExists{table_v2_multikernel.tex}{Table~\ref{tab:v2-multikernel} asks whether the kernel on the state inputs is the limiting choice, and it is
not. Among the ten kernels the spectral mixture and the Mat\'ern-5/2 tie on $Y_1$ ($0.089\%$) and the spectral
mixture is best on $Y_2$ and $Y_3$ ($0.237\%$ and $0.099\%$); the Mat\'ern-3/2 and the Gaussian are within a few
thousandths of a point on $Y_1$, the relevance-determination fits within two hundredths on $Y_2$ and a tenth on
$Y_3$; the arc-cosine kernels are two to six times worse; and the additive kernel fails outright ($4$ to $20\%$),
so no component is a sum of one-dimensional functions of the state. On the spherical albedo $Y_4$ every kernel but the
additive one sits between $2.3$ and $3.5\%$, the rough Mat\'ern-1/2 and the NTK at the low end. The convex kernel sum puts all of its
weight on one kernel in every lane, the kernel with the lowest validation error, and adds nothing. The network of
this table is a modest one, and its residual correction improves it by a third or more on the first three components
and by a tenth on $Y_4$ without reaching the best kernel, while the Mat\'ern-5/2 kernel on its last hidden layer
reaches $0.105\%$, $0.211\%$, $0.114\%$ and $2.30\%$: ahead of every input kernel on $Y_2$ and $Y_4$ and within two
hundredths of a point of the best on $Y_1$ and $Y_3$. The convex stack of all heads is the best predictor of the
table on every component ($0.066\%$, $0.156\%$, $0.077\%$ and $1.96\%$), $22$ to $26\%$ below the best single
head on $Y_1$ to $Y_3$ and nine percent below it on $Y_4$; the coordinatewise selection improves on no single head,
and the ridge stack only on $Y_3$. The spread over seeds is a few percent of the value for most heads and a tenth
for the Gaussian kernel on $Y_2$ and $Y_3$, whose length scale the validation rows select less stably.}{}

\IfFileExists{table_v2_perturbation.tex}{
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{\input{table_v2_perturbation}}
\caption{Same-data perturbation of the kernel predictor (Proposition~\ref{prop:perturb}): for Nystr\"om
approximations \cite{nystrom}, a changed nugget and compressed inputs or features, the signed spectrum of $B$, the median
movement of the prediction on held-out rows, and the ratios of the residual-action bound (ii), the signed-spectrum
bound (iii), the bound requiring $\|B\|<1$, and the ridge bound (iv) to that movement. A dash marks a bound that
does not apply.}
\label{tab:v2-perturbation}
\end{table}}{}

Table~\ref{tab:v2-perturbation} measures the perturbation bounds where the theorem allows them. The exact identity
of Proposition~\ref{prop:perturb}(i) holds to rounding at every system. Every bound holds at every held-out row.
The signed-spectrum bound is finite for a tenfold ridge increase, where $\|B\|$ is near nine, with the coefficient
$s/(\lambda_{\min}(H)+s)$ of item (iv); the bound that requires $\|B\|<1$ does not apply there. On the Nystr\"om
ladder of the input kernel the residual-action bound exceeds the median movement by a factor between $57$ and
$408$ and the signed-spectrum bound by $1{,}500$ to $4{,}000$, so the first is tighter by a factor of six to
seventy; on the feature kernels the same ratios are in the thousands and the tens of millions, the slack sitting in
the product of the whitened residual energy and the whitened query norm rather than in the eigenvalues. Compressed
inputs make $B$ indefinite with a least eigenvalue near $-1$, and there the residual-action bound, at $14$ to $64$
times the movement, is the only informative one.

\section{Synthetic reference for the transfer theorem}\label{sec:results-synthetic}

\IfFileExists{table_v2_synthetic.tex}{
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{\input{table_v2_synthetic}}
\caption{The model of Proposition~\ref{prop:attained} with $F_t(u)=u^\beta$, two million samples per point, the
constrained retrieval run as specified: the measured exponent of the mean-square reflectance error against
$\varepsilon_R^2$ for the average-error family against $\beta/(\beta+2)$, the measured and analytic slopes of the
uniform family on the same threshold ladder, the largest relative difference between the Monte Carlo and the
analytic curves of the uniform and profile families, and the number of entries at which the pointwise inequality
fails.}
\label{tab:v2-synthetic}
\end{table}}{}

Table~\ref{tab:v2-synthetic} is a check of the mathematics on manufactured data, not a result about the corpora.
The average-error exponents match $\beta/(\beta+2)$ to three digits. The uniform-family slopes fall below their
limits over the finite ladder, and the analytic curve on the same ladder gives the same slopes to three digits: at
$\beta=2$ the local slope is $2-2/(1+2\log(1/\varepsilon))$, which is $1.72$ on the ladder used. The Monte Carlo
agrees with the analytic curve of the profile family to at most five parts in ten thousand at every $\beta$, and with
that of the uniform family to three parts in a thousand except at $\beta=2$, where the difference is one part in a
hundred; the pointwise inequality holds at every one of the ten million samples.

\section{The matched benchmark and the transfer contrast}\label{sec:results-benchmarks}

\IfFileExists{table_v2_pkanrtm.tex}{
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{\input{table_v2_pkanrtm}}
\caption{The correction-coefficient corpus of \cite{pkan} under its own protocol: the release's state split
(35,000 / 7,500 / 7,500 states) and the paper's out-of-distribution split, whose test states lie above the 0.85
quantile of aerosol optical depth or of column water vapour, with the remaining states split 85/15; the paper's
categorical inputs, with and without the 6S \cite{vermote} coefficients as inputs; pooled RMSE, MAE, $R^2$ and SMAPE over the
three coefficients and thirteen bands, mean and standard deviation over three seeds (standard) or three
initialisations (OOD); the published values on the last rows.}
\label{tab:v2-pkanrtm}
\end{table}}{}

\IfFileExists{table_v2_oco2.tex}{
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{0.8\textwidth}{!}{\input{table_v2_oco2}}
\caption{OCO-2 \cite{eldering}: the heads of the seeded campaign (three training losses, the kernel and the ridge readout on each
network's features, the matched raw-input kernels) and four combination rules fitted on validation and read once
on test: the per-coordinate selection on the reduced error, the same selection on the exact radiance error, and
simplex stacks under each metric. Mean and standard deviation over seeds.}
\label{tab:v2-oco2}
\end{table}}{}

On the correction-coefficient corpus the comparison is made under the benchmark's protocol and metrics, and the
claim is improvement over the published values under that protocol and nothing wider. The residual-corrected
network improves on the published pKANrtm values in every one of the four metrics on both splits. On the release's
own split with the state inputs alone it reaches an RMSE of $0.00581\pm0.00004$ against the published $0.00619$, a
MAE of $0.00151$ against $0.00186$, $R^2=0.9982$ against $0.9947$ and a SMAPE of $3.54\%$ against $3.91\%$; with
the low-fidelity 6S coefficients as inputs, the benchmark paper's own construction, the same head reaches
$0.00578$, $0.00148$, $0.9982$ and $3.19\%$. Out of distribution the margin widens: $0.00620$ against the published
$0.01022$ in RMSE, $0.00252$ against $0.00544$ in MAE, $0.9980$ against $0.9942$ in $R^2$ and $3.37\%$ against
$5.40\%$ in SMAPE with the state inputs, and $0.00596$, $0.00232$, $0.9982$ and $2.92\%$ with the 6S inputs. The
ensemble without the correction is close behind the corrected head (RMSE $0.00591$ and MAE $0.00170$ on the
release's split, $0.00624$ and $0.00258$ out of distribution), the single network a little further back, and the
kernel on the network's features is the best of the kernels at
$0.0087$ (standard) and $0.0141$ (OOD); the kernels on the raw state and the ridge readout are an order of magnitude
worse, at $0.11$ to $0.12$, and the 6S inputs bring the raw-state kernel to $0.025$ (standard) and $0.029$ (OOD).
The standard deviations are over three seeds on the release's split and three initialisations on the
out-of-distribution split.

On OCO-2 the reduced-coefficient and radiance metrics order the heads differently, and Table~\ref{tab:v2-oco2}
measures by how much. The kernel on the network's features trained under the flat loss is the best single head in
the reduced coordinates ($4.1\%$, $16.3\%$ and $8.1\%$ on the O$_2$, weak CO$_2$ and strong CO$_2$ bands), but its
radiance error ($0.076\%$, $0.114\%$, $0.108\%$) is two to three times that of the same kernel on features trained
under a radiance-weighted loss ($0.031\%$, $0.048\%$, $0.064\%$), whose reduced errors are in turn four to six
times worse ($20$--$49\%$); the kernels on the raw state trail every feature kernel in both metrics ($29$--$59\%$
and $0.22$--$0.60\%$). The per-coordinate selection keeps the flat head's reduced error and takes the radiance error
to $0.028\%$, $0.051\%$ and $0.060\%$; selecting on the radiance error rather than on the coefficients picks the same
heads on two bands and changes one head on the third, to no measurable effect. The simplex stack under the reduced
metric holds the reduced error at the selection's level and lowers the radiance error further, to $0.029\%$,
$0.040\%$ and $0.054\%$; the stack fitted on the exact radiance error, a convex quadratic in the weights solved to a
KKT gap below $10^{-5}$, gives the lowest radiance error on every band ($0.026\%$, $0.039\%$, $0.051\%$), which is
three to nine percent below the reduced-metric stack, and pays for it entirely in coordinates that carry little
radiance: its reduced error is $18.6\%$ on O$_2$ and $37.4\%$ on weak CO$_2$ against $4.1\%$ and $16.3\%$, and
$8.9\%$ against $8.1\%$ on strong CO$_2$. Every rule is fitted on the 2,000 validation rows and read once on the
2,000 test rows; the standard deviations are over the three seeds.
